title: THE SOFT CADASTRE
subtitle: ATLANTA · A REGISTER OF CLAIMED EXTENT
premise: A cadastre records who holds which parcel, in hard lines. This one records what people and institutions claim about places — felt, contested, refused, forgotten — and holds every claim as bounded fuzzy extent that is never sharpened into a boundary it did not earn.

law.name: SOURCE ANCHOR ≠ TARGET
law.text: The place a sentence names is not the place it is about. 'Behind Ponce City Market' anchors on PCM and targets somewhere else. The anchor is recorded; the target is computed as a field, never asserted as a point.

law.name: THE COMPILER OWNS GEOMETRY
law.text: No model ever emits a coordinate. Language models emit closed-vocabulary anchors and relations. Deterministic code turns a relation into a kernel. A hallucinated relation is a wrong shape; a hallucinated coordinate is a lie with a decimal point.

law.name: ABSENCE IS NOT NEUTRALITY
law.text: Unmapped is not calm, safe, or fine. Blank grid means nobody spoke, or nobody was recorded speaking. Both surfaces refuse to shade absence.

law.name: THE UNRESOLVED IS KEPT
law.text: A place the gazetteer cannot resolve is stored with anchor:null and counted. Vernacular the alias table lacks is a measurement of the alias table, not of the city.

law.name: LOOK IS A GATE
law.text: The last gate is a human reading the frames. It cannot be passed by code, and the pipeline exits non-zero until a person has looked. A frame nobody read is a frame nobody checked.

law.name: FIXTURE DECLARES ITSELF
law.text: Synthetic and researcher-entered material is flagged in the data, on the map, and in this register. Provisional coordinates say PROVISIONAL everywhere they appear.

registries.state: FIXTURE. All 30 claims are authored test material, written to exercise the schema. An acquired corpus of 228 claims from the OpenStreetMap Notes API was built, audited and WITHDRAWN — see negative results. It remains on disk with its reason attached, because deleting rejected material would leave only the claim that it was rejected. A reference basemap is drawn beneath the field so a reader can tell where a claim is; it is geography, not evidence, and is excluded from every count.

surfaces.name: LOOK
surfaces.does: The gate surface. Halftone frames per topic with claim lines, territory boxes and refusal walls. Read every frame, press MARK READ, drop the downloaded ledger into ledger/look.jsonl. Gate 5 passes only after this.

registries.state: SAMPLE. The minutes are synthetic, written to exercise the pipeline, and the anchor coordinates are PROVISIONAL eyeball values. Extraction now runs on the operator tier — a model read each agenda item and emitted a relation program, validated against the closed vocabularies. Gates 1–4 pass; gate 5 fails until a human opens the viewer and reads every frame.

pipeline_seres.name: ACQUIRE
pipeline_seres.note: Public API, no key, no agreement. Tiles the city bbox and warns when a tile comes back full. Author usernames are deliberately not stored. NOTE: the corpus it was written for has been withdrawn — see negative results. The ingester is kept because the acquisition machinery is sound; what failed was the choice of source.

pipeline_seres.name: EXTRACT
pipeline_seres.note: Closed-vocabulary lexicon over note text. Every claim carries via:'lexicon' and confidence 0.55. Audited 2026-08-05: mostly false positives, one regex on the word 'park' producing 34% of all claims. The lesson is not that the lexicon was weak — it was declared weak — but that nobody read its output before it was published.

pipeline_seres.name: BASEMAP
pipeline_seres.note: Reference geography only — boundary, water, major road classes, rail and orienting place names. Stored under its own key, never in claims, and drawn in a neutral weight that cannot be mistaken for evidence. A field of claims with no ground under it is unreadable: 258 glowing points on a lat/lon grid say something was said somewhere and nothing else.

pipeline_seres.name: BUILD
pipeline_seres.makes: seres/data.json · data.embed.js · the helm's inline ATLAS
pipeline_seres.note: Composes every part for one city and gates it: ranges, polarity, geometry, evidence span, fixture flag, provenance. All three artifacts written together so none can disagree. One atlas per city — merging two would put one city's notes inside another's bbox and call it a region.

pipeline.name: FETCH
pipeline.note: Zero-dep. Saves PDFs, uses pdftotext if present, otherwise ledgers NEEDS-OCR. The gaps are data.

pipeline.name: SEGMENT
pipeline.note: Cut at the agenda item. Never at the paragraph.

pipeline.name: EXTRACT
pipeline.note: Three tiers, not two. --stub is regex. The API tier needs a key and a bill. The OPERATOR tier emits one fully-rendered prompt per unit for a model that is already reading the repository, and ingests its answer through a validator that refuses anything breaking the contract: an anchor or relation outside the closed list, a surface form not present verbatim in the unit, a co-mention naming an unresolved anchor, or any number describing space. A model in the loop is not trusted more than a model behind an API.

pipeline.name: COMPILE
pipeline.note: All geometry is made here, by code, from relations.

pipeline.name: GATE
pipeline.note: Exits 1 until every gate passes. Each failure names the stage that fixes it.

pipeline.name: BUILD SURFACES
pipeline.note: Inlines the compiled atlas at the __EMBED__ marker so both surfaces work from a double-click. This step had no script and was done by hand once, which meant every later compile left the surfaces showing an older world. A pipeline whose last step is manual is a pipeline that lies about its own output.

pipeline.name: LOOK
pipeline.note: A human. This is the point.

entries.name: Atlanta
entries.registry_ii: sample corpus, provisional anchors, gates 1–4 pass

portable: REGISTRY I whole. Acquisition, extraction, compose and gate are city-agnostic; a new city is a bbox, a tiling and a name.
The relation → kernel table. 'Behind' is a bearing and an offset anywhere.
The gate structure, including the ratio test and LOOK.
not_portable: The gazetteer. planOf is vernacular, and vernacular is the least transferable thing a city has.
The anchors and the grid — halfworld/world.config.json is forked per city, not parameterised.

The segmentation unit. Atlanta's NPU agenda item is a chartered review unit; New Orleans' NPP convenes per application, so 'the agenda item' does not cut the same way and a REGISTRY II there needs its own segmentation rule before any compute is spent.
The extraction lexicon, partly — regional vernacular for the same condition differs.

moves.name: Give Registry I a LOOK gate
moves.gain: The thing that would have caught this before it was published
moves.cost: One gate in build-atlas.mjs plus a reading surface. No acquisition, no API spend.
moves.how: Registry II refuses to pass until a human has read every frame. Registry I has no such gate and admitted 228 unreviewed claims. Sample n claims per dimension, require a human verdict on each, and fail the build until the verdicts exist.

moves.name: Read a corpus before compiling it
moves.gain: Avoids repeating the OSM Notes result on the next source
moves.cost: Ten minutes of reading raw text.
moves.how: Before writing an ingester, print fifty random rows of the source and read them. The OSM Notes corpus advertised itself in its own source-register blind-spot column — 'contributor population and task-focused language' — and that warning was under-weighted for a full acquisition cycle.

moves.name: ATL311
moves.gain: Actual service narratives — the corpus Registry I was designed for
moves.cost: A de-identified records request, and a privacy review of the free-text field before a single record is archived.
moves.how: Already requested and pending. Unlike map notes, these are people describing conditions in places. Read a sample before building anything.

moves.name: Turn on Registry II acquisition
moves.gain: The institutional lane, which no other source substitutes for
moves.cost: atlas/manifest.json with real NPU minutes URLs, plus OCR for the NPUs that post scans.
moves.how: fetch-minutes.mjs is written and waiting on that manifest. Minutes are unambiguously human statements about territory, which is what the corpus test above would have asked of any source.

moves.name: More cities
moves.gain: Comparison, and a test of which findings were ever about Atlanta
moves.cost: Registry I: a config file. Registry II: a forked world.config.json and a segmentation rule per institution.
moves.how: cities/new-orleans.json is the worked example, including what did not port.

other_datasets: OSM changeset comments — the same API family, contributor reasoning rather than reports.
Wikipedia/Wikidata place descriptions — ideal-type language, useful precisely as the limiting construct the schema already models.
Public transit rider feedback and MARTA board minutes — a second institutional lane with a different franchise.
Historic newspaper archives — the same claim schema over a time axis, which is where 'condition' stops being a time-of-day clause and becomes a decade.

negative_results.claim_tested: OpenStreetMap Notes are a vernacular testimony corpus — people reporting that the map and the ground disagree.
negative_results.how: Sampled the extracted claims per dimension and measured what share of the corpus is machine-written.
findings: The largest dimension, recreational_value, was 78 claims (34% of the corpus) from a single regex matching the word 'park'. Its top hits are the street name 'Park Bench Place, Mableton, GA 30126' and the instruction 'Park at the end of street'.
42% of claims derive from app-generated text: StreetComplete quest templates, Organic Maps POI reports, Scout app error reports.
Of the 1007 human-written notes, the great majority are map-editing requests, not statements about place.
Other false positives: 'cobblinc route 15 bus stop' scored transit_walk_advantage +1; a business listing containing the word 'damaged' scored maintenance_neglect.
negative_results.consequence: The bottleneck was never the extractor. An LLM extraction pass over this material would have bought more accurate classification of a map-maintenance queue. The part is withdrawn and the ranked plan corrected.
negative_results.cost_of_learning_it_late: The corpus was acquired, compiled, published and reported as a result before anyone read the text it contained.
negative_results.structural_cause: Registry II cannot pass its gates until a human reads every frame. Registry I had no equivalent gate, so 228 unreviewed claims went straight into the atlas.

negative_results.claim_tested: The regex --stub tier is good enough to flow the pipeline while the real translator waits for an API key.
negative_results.verdict: REFUTED — and the waiting was unnecessary
negative_results.how: Ran the LLM tier with the assistant already in the session as the operator, then diffed it against the stub on the same seven units.
findings: The stub emitted the same building three times per topic — 'THE OLD SEARS BUILDING', 'OLD SEARS BUILDING', 'SEARS BUILDING' — because the alias table matches overlapping substrings. 26 mentions collapsed to 20 real ones.

The stub read 'fronting the Eastside Trail' as relation 'behind'. It fronts the trail; the addition is behind the building and in front of the trail, which is two relations to two anchors in one sentence.
The stub resolved 'Ponce City Market' to the anchor ponce-de-leon-ave twice, because the alias PONCE matches inside it.
The stub emitted stances outside the closed vocabulary — 'approv' and 'no action' — and nothing in the pipeline checked. The operator validator rejects them.
The stub's possessive span was 'street'; the actual claim in the minutes is 'our street'. The pronoun is the whole point of a territorial claim.
negative_results.consequence: The operator tier costs no API key and no separate spend. It should have been the default from the first run, and the stub kept only for offline smoke tests.
negative_results.cost_of_learning_it_late: Every compiled field, every published frame and the whole first LOOK surface was built from the regex tier.
negative_results.structural_cause: The harness offered '--stub or an API key' and nobody asked whether a model was already present.

negative_results.claim_tested: The unit's dominant anchor — the one mentioned most — is the right place to sit a refusal wall or a territory box.
negative_results.how: The cleaner extraction made a segment dominant, and the refusal wall for a plainly denied variance silently vanished from the compiled output.
findings: Dominance by raw mention count rewards repetition, which is exactly what the regex tier's overlapping aliases produced. The stub 'won' the wall by accident.
Walls and boxes can only sit on a point anchor, and the compiler skipped them without a word when the dominant anchor was a street.
negative_results.consequence: compile-field.mjs now prefers the dominant anchor, falls back to the best point anchor in the same unit, and records a drop when the unit has no point anchor at all. Walls went 0 → 1 and boxes 2 → 4.
negative_results.cost_of_learning_it_late: A better extraction made the output worse, which is the failure mode hardest to notice.
negative_results.structural_cause: A silent skip. Everywhere else this system logs what it drops; this path did not.
